topics.title: Meaning, Objectives, and Sources of Buy-Back
explain: Buy-back means a company repurchasing its own outstanding shares or specified securities.
Shares bought back must be cancelled, resulting in a reduction of share capital.
A company is prohibited from purchasing its own shares for investment purposes.

Key objectives include increasing Earnings Per Share (EPS), boosting promoter holdings, preventing hostile takeovers, supporting market price in a depressed market, and returning surplus cash to shareholders.
Allowed sources for buy-back are free reserves, securities premium account, or proceeds of a fresh issue of any shares or specified securities.
No buy-back of any class of shares can be made out of proceeds of an earlier fresh issue of the same class of shares.

flow.title: Process of Funding a Buy-Back
steps: Identify surplus cash or required funds
Check available Free Reserves and Securities Premium
Issue different class of securities if required
Repurchase own shares from permitted sources
Cancel repurchased shares immediately

topics.example: A company with Rs 50 lakhs in securities premium and free reserves buys back 10,000 of its own equity shares using these reserves to improve its EPS.
remember: Buy-back cannot be funded using proceeds from a fresh issue of the SAME class of shares.
mistakes: Assuming revaluation reserve or unrealized gain reserves can be used as free reserves for buy-back.

quiz.q: Which source CANNOT be used to buy back equity shares?
o: Proceeds of fresh issue of equity shares
Proceeds of fresh issue of preference shares
quiz.why: Section 68(1) prohibits using proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares for buy-back.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a primary objective of a share buy-back?
quiz.why: Reducing the total number of outstanding shares increases EPS if overall earnings remain constant.

topics.title: Conditions and Restrictions for Buy-Back
explain: Buy-back must be authorized by the Articles of Association (AOA) of the company.
A Special Resolution passed at a general meeting is required for buy-back.
Exception: Only a Board Resolution is needed if the buy-back is up to 10% of total paid-up equity capital plus free reserves.
All shares or specified securities intended for buy-back must be fully paid-up.
There must be a minimum gap of one year between the closure of one buy-back offer and the offer of another.
Under Section 70, a company cannot buy back shares through any subsidiary company or investment company.
Section 70 prohibits buy-back if there is a subsisting default in repayment of deposits, term loans, debentures, or dividends, unless default is remedied and 3 years have elapsed since cessation.

flow.title: Eligibility & Authorization Check
steps: Verify authorization in Articles of Association
Ensure all shares for buy-back are fully paid-up
Check required resolution type based on percentage
Confirm no active defaults under Section 70
Verify 1 year gap from previous buy-back closure

topics.example: A company wanting to buy back 8% of its equity capital passes a Board Resolution without needing a Special Resolution or AOA amendment.
remember: Board Resolution limit = up to 10% of (Equity + Free Reserves); Special Resolution limit = up to 25% of (Capital + Free Reserves).
mistakes: Assuming a company can buy back shares immediately after clearing a loan default without waiting for the 3-year statutory cooling period.

quiz.q: What is the maximum limit of buy-back that can be approved solely by a Board Resolution?
o: 10% of paid-up equity capital + free reserves
quiz.why: Section 68(2) allows up to 10% of paid-up equity capital plus free reserves via a Board Resolution.

quiz.q: If a company remedies a default in term loan repayment, after how many years can it proceed with a buy-back?
quiz.why: Section 70(1) requires 3 years to elapse from the cessation of default before a buy-back is allowed.

topics.title: Procedural and Compliance Requirements
explain: Notice of general meeting must contain an explanatory statement disclosing material facts, necessity, class of security, invested amount, and time limit.
Every buy-back must be completed within 12 months from passing the resolution.
Buy-back can be made from existing shareholders on a proportionate basis, open market, or stock options/sweat equity.
A Declaration of Solvency verified by affidavit must be filed with ROC and SEBI (for listed companies) before making the buy-back.
Bought-back securities must be extinguished and physically destroyed within 7 days of completion.
No further issue of the same kind of shares is permitted within 6 months, except bonus issues or existing conversion obligations.
A register of buy-back must be maintained, and a return filed with ROC/SEBI within 30 days of completion.
Nominal value of shares bought back out of free reserves or securities premium must be transferred to Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR).

flow.title: Timeline of Buy-Back Procedures
steps: Pass Resolution with Explanatory Statement
File Declaration of Solvency with ROC/SEBI
Complete Buy-Back within 12 months
Destroy share certificates within 7 days
Transfer Nominal Value to CRR Account
File Buy-Back Return within 30 days

topics.example: ABC Ltd completes its buy-back offer on 1st May, destroys the physical share certificates by 8th May, and files a return with ROC within 30 days.
remember: 7 days to extinguish shares; 12 months to complete buy-back; 6 months prohibition on fresh issues; 30 days to file ROC return.
mistakes: Forgetting to transfer an amount equal to the nominal value of shares bought back from free reserves to the CRR account.

quiz.q: Within how many days of completion must a company extinguish and physically destroy shares bought back?
quiz.why: Section 68(6) mandates extinguishing and physically destroying securities within 7 days of completion.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time limit allowed to complete a buy-back process after passing the resolution?
quiz.why: Section 68(3) states that every buy-back must be completed within 12 months from the date of passing the resolution.

topics.title: The Three Statutory Tests for Maximum Buy-Back
explain: Test 1: Shares Outstanding Test — Buy-back cannot exceed 25% of the total paid-up equity shares in that financial year.
Test 2: Resource Test — Total amount invested in buy-back cannot exceed 25% of total paid-up capital plus free reserves.
Test 3: Debt-Equity Ratio Test — Debt (both long-term and short-term) post buy-back must not exceed twice the paid-up capital plus free reserves (2:1 ratio).
When CRR transfer 'x' and maximum buy-back 'y' mutually affect future equity, simultaneous equations are used: (Present Equity - x) - Minimum Equity = y, and x = (Nominal Value / Offer Price) * y.
The maximum permissible number of shares for buy-back is the LEAST result among all three tests.

flow.title: Calculating Maximum Permissible Buy-Back
steps: Calculate Shares Outstanding limit (25% of Equity Shares)
Calculate Resource limit (25% of Capital + Free Reserves)
Calculate Debt-Equity limit (Debt/Equity <= 2:1)
Apply simultaneous equations if CRR affects future equity
Select the LEAST of the three test results

topics.example: If Test 1 allows 30,000 shares, Test 2 allows 25,000 shares, and Test 3 allows 20,000 shares, the company can buy back a maximum of 20,000 shares.
remember: Debt includes both long-term and short-term debt; Equity post buy-back excludes CRR transfer.
mistakes: Excluding short-term debt when calculating total debt for the Debt-Equity Ratio Test.

quiz.q: What is the maximum post buy-back Debt-to-Equity ratio allowed under Section 68(2)(d)?
quiz.why: The ratio of debt owed by the company after buy-back cannot be more than twice the capital and free reserves (2:1).

quiz.q: Under the Shares Outstanding Test, what is the maximum percentage of equity shares a company can buy back in an FY?
quiz.why: Section 68(2)(c) restricts buy-back of equity shares in any financial year to 25% of total paid-up equity capital.

topics.title: Accounting Treatment and Journal Entries
explain: If assets/investments are sold to generate cash, record sale and recognize profit/loss in Profit & Loss A/c.
Record amount due on buy-back: Debit Equity Share Capital A/c (nominal value), Debit Premium Payable on Buy-Back A/c (excess price), and Credit Equity Shares Buy-Back A/c.
Record payment: Debit Equity Shares Buy-Back A/c and Credit Bank A/c.
Adjust premium paid on buy-back against Securities Premium or Free Reserves (General Reserve / Profit & Loss A/c).
Transfer face value of shares bought back out of free reserves to Capital Redemption Reserve A/c (Revenue Reserve/P&L A/c Dr. To Capital Redemption Reserve A/c).
CRR can subsequently be utilized ONLY for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares to members.

flow.title: Journal Entry Sequence for Buy-Back
steps: Record sale of investments/assets if cash needed
Debit Share Capital and Premium Payable; Credit Buy-back A/c
Debit Buy-back A/c and Credit Bank A/c for payment
Debit Reserves to write off Premium Payable
Debit Free Reserves and Credit CRR A/c for nominal value
Debit CRR A/c and Credit Share Capital for bonus issue

topics.example: Shares of nominal value Rs 10 are bought back at Rs 30. Share Capital is debited by Rs 10, Premium Payable by Rs 20, and Buy-Back A/c credited by Rs 30.
remember: Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) can ONLY be used for issuing fully paid bonus shares.
mistakes: Crediting Capital Reserve instead of Capital Redemption Reserve when transferring nominal value of bought back shares.

quiz.q: Which account is credited to transfer the nominal value of shares bought back out of free reserves?
quiz.why: Section 69(1) requires transferring a sum equal to the nominal value of shares purchased to Capital Redemption Reserve Account.

quiz.q: Capital Redemption Reserve created during buy-back can be utilized for which specific purpose?
quiz.why: Under Section 69(2), CRR can only be applied in paying up unissued shares to be issued as fully paid bonus shares.
